title: Guillain-Barre Syndrome in a patient with uterine adenocarcinoma undergoing treatment with immune-checkpoint inhibitor therapy: A case report and review of the literature
case_prompt:
A 72-year-old woman with stage IVB uterine adenocarcinoma presented with acute progressive weakness seven days after her second cycle of pembrolizumab and lenvatinib. Her cancer history included initial neoadjuvant carboplatin–paclitaxel with radiographic response, a delay in surgery due to COVID-19 and tamoxifen therapy, and disease progression on follow-up CT with rising CA-125.  
She reported new onset shortness of breath, odynophagia, worsening fatigue, diffuse myalgias, inability to walk, a generalized rash, and urinary retention.  
On examination, she was afebrile with normal vital signs. Neurologic evaluation revealed lower extremity strength 3/5, upper extremity strength 4/5, hyporeflexia, ataxia, and bilateral hand tremor. She could not void voluntarily. Laboratory studies showed a TSH of 14.0 mcIU/mL with a normal free T4.  
She was admitted and started on levothyroxine, a tapering dose of oral dexamethasone, nystatin suspension, and supportive care. By hospital day 5, her fatigue had improved but she remained unable to void, required assistance to ambulate, and continued to have ataxia, hyporeflexia, and tremor. Non-contrast CT of the head and MRI of the brain and lumbar spine revealed no acute abnormalities.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Metastatic disease progression was considered but imaging showed no focal lesions to explain her neurologic deficits — “Non-contrast CT of the head and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and lumbar spine did not reveal any abnormal findings.”  
2. Paraneoplastic neuropathy was included in the initial differential — “Differential diagnosis includes metastatic disease progression, paraneoplastic disease, or infectious etiologies.”  
3. Infectious etiologies were also on the differential given the subacute presentation — “Differential diagnosis includes metastatic disease progression, paraneoplastic disease, or infectious etiologies.”  
4. Other immune checkpoint inhibitor–related neurologic adverse events such as myasthenia gravis were possible but the pattern favored a peripheral demyelinating process — “Neurological events including myasthenia gravis, GBS, chronic immune demyelinating polyneuropathy, encephalitis, myositis, neuritis, and enteric neuropathy have all been associated with ICIs.”  
5. Guillain–Barre syndrome was diagnosed based on albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF and demyelinating features on nerve conduction studies — “Lumbar puncture ... revealed mild albuminocytologic dissociation and mildly elevated protein ... Nerve conduction studies demonstrated mixed axonal and demyelinating features and conduction block concerning for Guillain-Barre Syndrome (GBS)…”  
6. Pembrolizumab was identified as the likely trigger due to the temporal relation and its known association with neurologic irAEs — “Pembrolizumab was suspected to be the causative agent due to its known association with immune-related adverse events (irAEs), and specifically neurologic complications.”
